stem: Which of the following is NOT an indication for intubation and ventilation in a child with severe bronchiolitis?
explanation: Severe bronchiolitis may require intubation for hypoxaemia, apnoeas, exhaustion, or ventilatory failure. Severe metabolic alkalosis is not a typical indication for intubation and ventilation.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The item already contains a single best answer among the existing options; option E is the only one that is not an indication for intubation/ventilation in severe bronchiolitis.

optionExplanations.A: Severe hypoxaemia is an indication for ventilatory support.
optionExplanations.B: Inability to protect the airway is a standard indication for intubation.
optionExplanations.C: Rising PaCO2 suggests ventilatory failure and may require intubation.
optionExplanations.D: Recurrent apnoea is an indication for escalation to ventilation.
optionExplanations.E: This is not a recognised indication for intubation in bronchiolitis.

source.questionTextHtml:
Which of the following IS NOT an indication of intubation and ventilation in a child with severe bronchiolitis?

PaO2 <50mmHg

Instructions

The following nine questions refer to Patrick’s clinical scenario.

Clinical scenario 1 - Patrick

Patrick, a six month old infant, is brought to the emergency department with wheezing and respiratory distress. On examination he has severe chest wall retractions, grunting and is pale. His vital signs are:

RR 80/min, HR 190/min, temperature 38.0’C, SaO2 80% in room air.

The accompanying table has the normal ranges indicated in the 2010 NSW Health Standard Paediatric Observation Chart, SPOC.

Patrick has wheeze and crackles throughout his chest. There is a history of having been snuffly with a cough for the last two days. The entire family has a cold.
